input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-605: Advanced Object-Oriented Programming Concepts. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course focuses on identifying advanced object-oriented programming concepts and implementing them in the context of specific problems. This course covers advanced concepts such as event-driven programming, design patterns, distributed and concurrent programming, and the use, design and implementation of applications. Assignments (both in class and as homework) requiring a solution to a problem and an implementation in code are an integral part of the course. Note: This course serves as a bridge course for graduate students and cannot be taken by undergraduate students without permission from the CS Undergraduate Program Coordinator. This course is restricted to students in COMPSCI-MS. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[java-language-specification]
The Java language specification defines classes, objects, interfaces, inheritance, method invocation, fields, access control, exceptions, generics, and concurrency semantics. A class declares state and behavior, while an object is an instance with its own runtime identity and field state. Interfaces declare contracts that classes may implement. Inheritance reuses and specializes behavior, but dynamic method dispatch selects an implementation from the runtime class of the receiver. Access modifiers control which declarations are visible. Exceptions separate normal results from abrupt completion. Generic types express reusable abstractions while preserving compile-time type constraints. Object-oriented design should make responsibilities, invariants, dependencies, composition, and substitution behavior explicit.

[python-data-model]
Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Classes create user-defined types whose instances can contain attributes and participate in operations through special methods. Attribute lookup follows defined rules across an instance and its class hierarchy. Methods bind functions to instances. Inheritance allows a class to derive behavior from base classes, while composition connects objects through explicit attributes. Mutable and immutable objects have different state behavior. Exceptions communicate failures through defined control flow. A sound object model states ownership, invariants, public operations, extension points, and observable behavior rather than relying on hidden shared state.

This course focuses on identifying advanced object-oriented programming concepts and implementing them in the context of specific problems. This course covers advanced concepts such as event-driven programming, design patterns, distributed and concurrent programming, and the use, design and implementation of applications. Assignments (both in class and as homework) requiring a solution to a problem and an implementation in code are an integral part of the course. beats.claim: Objects possess a unique runtime identity and encapsulated field state that persists across method invocations.
beats.example: A `User` instance maintains its own `username` and `sessionToken` values independent of other `User` instances.
beats.title: Foundations of Object Identity and State
beats.visualDirection: Display a side-by-side comparison of two `User` objects with distinct memory addresses and separate field values, highlighting encapsulation boundaries.

beats.claim: Inheritance reuses and specializes behavior through class hierarchies, while composition connects objects through explicit attributes to promote flexible design.
beats.example: A `Vehicle` base class provides `move()` logic, but a `DeliveryTruck` composes a `CargoContainer` object instead of inheriting from `Truck` to avoid rigid hierarchies.
beats.title: Inheritance versus Composition for Reuse
beats.visualDirection: Show a class diagram contrasting a deep inheritance tree with a flat composition graph, using arrows to indicate 'has-a' relationships.

beats.claim: Dynamic method dispatch selects an implementation from the runtime class of the receiver, enabling polymorphic behavior without compile-time type knowledge.
beats.example: Calling `draw()` on a `Shape` reference invokes `Circle.draw()` or `Square.draw()` depending on the actual object at runtime.
beats.title: Dynamic Method Dispatch and Polymorphism
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a method call flow where a generic `Shape` reference routes to distinct `Circle` and `Square` implementations, emphasizing runtime resolution.

beats.claim: Access modifiers control which declarations are visible, ensuring that internal state remains protected and only authorized operations modify it.
beats.example: A `BankAccount` class exposes `deposit()` and `withdraw()` methods while keeping the `balance` field private to prevent unauthorized modification.
beats.title: Encapsulation and Access Control
beats.visualDirection: Render a class interface with public methods highlighted and private fields shaded, showing how access control restricts direct state access.

beats.claim: Exceptions separate normal results from abrupt completion, allowing structured error propagation without interrupting normal control flow.
beats.example: A `NetworkRequest` throws a `ConnectionTimeoutException` when a server fails to respond, allowing the caller to handle the failure gracefully.
beats.title: Exceptions for Error Handling
beats.visualDirection: Map a control flow diagram showing a normal execution path branching into an exception handler block when a timeout occurs.

beats.claim: Generic types express reusable abstractions while preserving compile-time type constraints, preventing runtime type mismatches in collections and utilities.
beats.example: A `Queue<T>` class ensures that only elements of type `T` are added or removed, eliminating the need for runtime casting.
beats.title: Generics for Type-Safe Abstractions
beats.visualDirection: Show a generic collection diagram with type parameters `T` and `U`, highlighting how compile-time checks enforce type safety.

beats.claim: Event-driven programming decouples components by allowing objects to react to asynchronous occurrences through registered callbacks and message queues.
beats.example: A `UIController` registers a `Button` instance to emit `click` events, triggering a `EventHandler` without direct method calls.
beats.title: Event-Driven Programming Principles
beats.visualDirection: Draw a publisher-subscriber diagram showing an event source broadcasting to multiple independent listeners via a message bus.

beats.claim: Design patterns provide proven structural templates that solve recurring design problems by standardizing object interactions and system architecture.
beats.example: The `Strategy` pattern allows a `PaymentProcessor` to swap `CreditCard` and `Crypto` algorithms at runtime without modifying the core class.
beats.title: Design Patterns for Structural Integrity
beats.visualDirection: Present a before-and-after class diagram showing how a rigid hierarchy is replaced by a flexible strategy interface and implementations.

beats.claim: Concurrent programming manages simultaneous execution through shared memory or message passing, while distributed programming coordinates independent processes across networked or-
beats.example: A `TaskScheduler` uses thread pools to process independent jobs concurrently, ensuring that shared resources are accessed via synchronized locks or immutable data structures.
beats.title: Concurrent and Distributed Programming Foundations
beats.visualDirection: Render a concurrent execution model with multiple threads accessing a shared resource, highlighting synchronization mechanisms like mutexes or atomic variables.

beats.claim: Effective implementation requires verifying that responsibilities are explicit, invariants are maintained, dependencies are minimized, and substitution behavior is preserved.
beats.example: Before deploying a `DataProcessor`, developers check that each class has a single responsibility, validates that internal state cannot be corrupted, and confirms that subclasses can replace base classes without breaking contracts.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist for Implementation
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist graphic with checkboxes for 'Single Responsibility', 'Invariant Validation', 'Dependency Minimization', and 'Substitution Compliance', ready for instructor review.

Explain how dynamic method dispatch and encapsulation enforce runtime polymorphism and data integrity.
Apply design patterns and event-driven principles to structure complex, maintainable software systems.
